1.title: Deploying, Operating and the Global Infrastructure
1.text: Welcome to Module six: Deploying, Operating and the Global Infrastructure. This module opens the third domain of the exam, Cloud Technology and Services, with task statements three point one and three point two. You will learn how people and programs reach A W S, how to build the same environment again and again, and where A W S physically runs: Regions, Availability Zones and edge locations.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. Choose among the console, the C L I, S D Ks and infrastructure as code, for one-time and repeatable work. Explain what A W S CloudFormation, A W S Service Catalog and Service Quotas do. Tell cloud, hybrid and on-premises deployment models apart. Describe Regions, Availability Zones and edge locations, and how they relate. And decide when to use multiple Availability Zones, and when to use multiple Regions.

1.title: Case Check-In: Tidewater Goes Global
1.text: Back to Tidewater Outfitters. Its customers in Europe see slow pages, and the team wants a second copy of the shop near them. Engineers build servers by clicking through the console, and no two environments match. Test and production must be identical, and quick to rebuild. The warehouse system stays in the back office, but it must still talk to the cloud. Your job is to choose how to deploy, operate and place the shop.

1.title: Ways to Reach AWS
1.text: There are several ways to reach A W S, and the exam expects you to know them. The A W S Management Console is a web-based interface for people. It is good for exploring and for one-time tasks. The A W S Command Line Interface, the C L I, runs commands in a shell, so steps can be scripted and automated. A W S S D Ks are libraries for languages such as Python, Java and JavaScript, so applications can call A W S services. The C L I and the S D Ks call the A W S service A P Is directly, and if you send A P I requests yourself, you must also sign them. A W S CloudShell gives you the C L I in a browser tab, already signed in, though it is beyond the exam guide. Exam tip: everything in the console is also available through the A P I, the C L I and the S D Ks.

1.title: Console, CLI, SDK or Template?
1.text: How do you choose? Look at what Tidewater needs. To try a new service once, use the Management Console. It is visual, needs no code, and suits one-time work. To run the same steps every night, use an A W S C L I script, because commands can be saved, shared and scheduled. To let the shop's own code create or read resources, use an A W S S D K, which calls A W S from your application. And to build the same whole environment every time, use infrastructure as code, because a template makes it repeatable. The rule of thumb: a one-time operation is fine in the console; a repeatable process should be scripted or put in a template. Exam tip: one-time and visual means console; repeat and automate means C L I, S D K or a template.

1.title: Infrastructure as Code: AWS CloudFormation
1.text: Infrastructure as code means describing your infrastructure in text files that a tool turns into real resources. A W S CloudFormation does this. A CloudFormation template is a Y A M L or J S O N file that lists resources and their settings. A stack is everything created from one template, and you create, update and delete it as one unit. A change set previews an update before you apply it, and if creation fails, CloudFormation rolls back. The big benefit is reuse. Use one template for test and production, or in several Regions, and keep it in version control so you can track and reverse changes. The A W S C D K lets you write the same thing in a programming language, but that is beyond the exam guide. Exam tip: repeatable, consistent environments from a template point to A W S CloudFormation.

1.title: Service Catalog and Service Quotas
1.text: Two more management services appear in this task statement. A W S Service Catalog lets an organization create catalogs of approved I T services. Products are gathered in portfolios, and users can launch only approved products, within the constraints you set. Remember it as approved, standard setups through self-service. Service Quotas lets you view and manage your quotas, which are also called limits, from one place, and request increases. Picture a launch that fails because an account or Region limit was reached. Each service sets default quotas per account or Region, and some are adjustable. A W S Support might approve, deny or partly approve a request. Exam tip: approved products for users, Service Catalog; limits and increase requests, Service Quotas.

1.title: Deployment Models: Cloud, Hybrid and On-Premises
1.text: The exam asks about three deployment models. In a cloud deployment, all parts of the application run in the cloud. It was either built there or migrated, and you get the full benefit of the cloud. A hybrid deployment connects cloud resources to existing resources that are not in the cloud, most often on-premises. It fits when some systems must stay on site, or when you move step by step. An on-premises deployment, sometimes called a private cloud, keeps resources in your own data center, using virtualization and management tools. It offers dedicated resources but few cloud benefits. A W S has services that help with hybrid, and they come later: Direct Connect and V P N, a virtual private network, in Module ten, Storage Gateway in Module eight, and A W S Outposts in Module seven. Exam tip: some systems in the cloud and some in your own data center, connected, is hybrid.

1.title: Regions, Availability Zones and Edge Locations
1.text: Now the global infrastructure. A Region is a physical location where A W S clusters data centers. Each Region has at least three isolated Availability Zones. An Availability Zone, or A Z, is one or more discrete data centers with redundant power, networking and connectivity. Edge locations are different. They sit in many more places than Regions, and they deliver content close to users. Look at the figure: the Region contains the zones, and the edge locations sit outside it. As of the fourth of November, twenty twenty-six, A W S reports thirty-nine Regions, one hundred twenty-four Availability Zones, and more than seven hundred fifty CloudFront points of presence. Counts change, and other A W S pages differ, and the exam does not test the numbers. Exam tip: a Region contains Availability Zones; edge locations are separate and serve cached content.

1.title: Choosing a Region
1.text: How do you choose a Region? Start with compliance and data residency. You choose the Region where your content is stored, and A W S will not move it out of that Region except as needed to provide the services or to comply with the law. Next, latency: pick a Region close to most of your users. Then services and features. Not every service is in every Region, so check availability. Cost matters too, so compare prices between Regions, which Module thirteen covers. Remember that Regions are independent, and each is isolated from the others. One extra detail beyond the guide: newer Regions must be enabled in your account before you can use them. Exam tip: if data must stay in a country, choose a Region there; if users are far away, choose a Region near them.

2.title: Availability Zones and High Availability
2.text: High availability means the application keeps working when a part of it fails. Availability Zones are how you get it. Each zone has its own power, cooling and physical security, so zones do not share a single point of failure. They are many kilometers apart, yet within one hundred kilometers, or sixty miles, joined by low-latency, high-bandwidth links, and the traffic between them is encrypted. So run your application in at least two zones, behind a load balancer. In the figure, one zone has failed, and the other two keep serving customers. Exam tip: to survive a data center failure inside a Region, use multiple Availability Zones.

2.title: Multiple Regions: When and Why
2.text: When do you need more than one Region? There are three reasons the exam likes. First, disaster recovery and business continuity: the shop keeps serving if a whole Region is unavailable, for example with a copy in a second Region. Second, low latency: users are served from a Region near them, such as a Europe Region for European customers. Third, data sovereignty: data stays in a chosen country to meet the law, so customer records are kept in a Region inside that country. Running in several Regions makes it important to copy your setup, and one CloudFormation template can build the same stack in each Region. Exam tip: a whole-Region failure, distance from users or legal location means multiple Regions; one data center failing means multiple Availability Zones.

2.title: Edge Locations: Content Close to Users
2.text: Edge locations, also called CloudFront points of presence, keep cached copies of your content near viewers. D N S sends each request to the edge location that serves it best, usually the nearest in latency. If the object is in the cache, that is a cache hit, and the edge returns it. If it is not, that is a cache miss. The edge fetches the object from the origin, such as an Amazon S three bucket, and caches it for next time. Regional edge caches sit between the origin and the edge locations and keep content longer. Amazon CloudFront uses all of this, and Module ten covers it. A W S Local Zones, beyond the guide, place some services closer to big cities. Exam tip: faster delivery of content to distant users means edge locations, through CloudFront.

2.title: What the Exam Asks: Deploying and Global Infrastructure
2.text: Here is how the exam frames this module. Console, C L I, S D K or template: explore once, script it, call it from code, or rebuild the same environment. One-time or repeatable: the console for one-time, and the C L I, an S D K or a template for repeatable. CloudFormation, Service Catalog or Service Quotas: build from a template, offer approved products, or manage limits. Cloud, hybrid or on-premises: all in A W S, connected to your data center, or only in your data center. Region, A Z or edge location: where data lives, a data center group inside a Region, or where cached content is served. And multi-A Z or multi-Region: survive a data center failure, or survive a Region failure and reach distant users. Exam tip: match the failure or the need to the smallest unit that solves it.

2.title: Design Check: Tidewater Goes Global
2.text: Now a design check. Cover the right column and answer each row yourself. Test and production that match exactly: a CloudFormation template, with one stack per environment. A nightly job that starts and stops test servers: an A W S C L I or S D K script on a schedule. Engineers exploring a new service for the first time: the Management Console. Only approved server setups for the support team: A W S Service Catalog. A launch fails because the account hit a limit: Service Quotas, then request an increase. The warehouse system stays on site but talks to the cloud: a hybrid deployment. The shop survives the loss of one data center: servers in two or more zones behind a load balancer. And product photos load slowly in Europe: CloudFront edge locations, and a Europe Region. Pause the video if you want more time.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. For access, the console is for people and one-time work, and the C L I and S D Ks call the same A P Is for scripts and applications. For infrastructure as code, CloudFormation builds consistent stacks from Y A M L or J S O N templates. For governance, Service Catalog offers approved products, and Service Quotas manages limits. For deployment models, there are cloud, hybrid, which is cloud plus your own data center, and on-premises. For global infrastructure, Regions hold at least three Availability Zones, and edge locations serve cached content. And for resilience, use multiple zones for a data center failure, and multiple Regions for a Region failure, low latency or data sovereignty.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. Tidewater needs the same load balancer, servers and database created identically in a test account and a production account, and rebuilt quickly when needed. Which approach fits best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Describe the resources in a CloudFormation template and build a stack from it. A template describes the resources once, and each stack built from it is consistent and repeatable. Manual steps and commands typed from memory drift between environments, and Service Quotas manages limits rather than copying settings.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. A developer wants to automate a nightly task that starts and stops test servers by running the same steps on a schedule. Which approach fits best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Write a script that uses the A W S C L I or an A W S S D K, and run it on a schedule. They call the A W S A P Is from code, so the steps can be saved, repeated and scheduled. The console is for one-time and visual work, and Service Catalog offers approved products rather than scheduled tasks.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. Tidewater keeps its warehouse system in its own data center and connects it to its resources in A W S. Which deployment model is this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A, hybrid. A hybrid deployment connects cloud-based resources with existing resources that are not in the cloud, most often on-premises. A cloud deployment runs every part in A W S, an on-premises deployment uses no cloud, and multi-Region describes where copies run rather than a deployment model.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. What is an A W S Availability Zone? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. An Availability Zone is one or more discrete data centers with redundant power, networking and connectivity in an A W S Region. Caching content near viewers describes an edge location, and an A W S account is a different concept altogether.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. Tidewater runs its web servers in one Availability Zone, and an outage there would take the shop offline. What is the simplest way to improve availability? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Run the web servers in two Availability Zones behind a load balancer. Zones do not share a single point of failure, so servers in two zones keep serving if one fails. A bigger instance, another account or an edge location in front still leave every server in the one zone that failed.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. Tidewater's European customers see slow loads of product photos that are stored in a Region in the United States. Which approach delivers the photos faster? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Use Amazon CloudFront to cache the photos at edge locations near them. The photos then travel a shorter distance. Another zone in the same Region adds resilience rather than proximity, CloudTrail records activity, and larger servers do not shorten the distance.

2.title: Practice Question 7
2.text: Question seven. Select two. Which two are valid reasons to run a workload in more than one A W S Region? The five options are on the screen. The answers are B and D. Multiple Regions support disaster recovery and business continuity, and they let you place data in a country to satisfy data sovereignty rules. Low latency for distant users is a third reason. Backups, encryption and Availability Zones are still needed, and I A M users are not shared between accounts automatically.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all seven answers. Question one: B. Question two: C. Question three: A. Question four: D. Question five: B. Question six: A. Question seven: B and D. That completes Module six. Next, Module seven covers the compute services: virtual servers, containers and serverless functions.
